screens.title: Health Systems and Game State Management
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to give characters a clear life cycle and how to coordinate the whole game's state. We'll define what a health system tracks, how to safely apply damage and healing so values never go out of bounds, and how to surface those changes to UI and gameplay events. Then we'll introduce a single authoritative GameManager using the Singleton pattern to track score, subscribe to player death, and move the game between Playing and GameOver states. This matters because predictable health behavior prevents bugs like negative health or overhealing, while a single GameManager prevents duplicated logic and keeps transitions consistent across scenes. As a concrete example, you'll implement a HealthSystem script that clamps current health between zero and a maximum, fires events on change, and calls Die when health reaches zero. Then you'll create a GameManager that persists across scene loads, exposes AddScore, and pauses the game on player death. Watch for common mistakes: initializing Singletons in the wrong lifecycle method and allowing negative or out-of-range values. By the end, you'll be able to wire coins, hazards, health, and score together in a robust way.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will be able to design and implement a basic health system, apply damage and healing safely, and connect health to UI and gameplay events. You will also implement a persistent GameManager as a Singleton that tracks score, subscribes to player death, and transitions the game state to GameOver or Win as appropriate. Each objective includes a small, practical skill: writing the TakeDamage and Heal methods so health never leaves the 0-to-max range; using events to update health bars; and coding Awake to establish a Singleton that persists across scenes. These skills matter for prototyping because they turn moment-to-moment interactions into predictable systems. A concrete example is clamping health using Mathf. Clamp to prevent overheal or negative life. A common misconception is that any global static field is a safe Singleton; instead, initializing the Instance in Awake and guarding duplicates avoids null access and unexpected duplicates. Practice will reinforce how to wire health events to UI and how the GameManager centralizes score changes and game flow.

screens.title: Health System Essentials
screens.narratorSegment: A health system is the mechanism that records a character's vitality and responds to changes. At its heart you maintain a maximum health and a current health value; you initialize current health to max in Start so the character begins at full vitality. The critical implementation detail is to guard modifications: never allow current health to drop below zero or exceed the maximum. Using a property setter that clamps values is robust because all health changes funnel through one place. For example, setting currentHealth via a private field and using Mathf. Clamp ensures any call to TakeDamage or Heal respects limits. Emit a health-changed event on every update so UI elements can subscribe and refresh the health bar automatically. A common misconception is to update UI directly from multiple scripts; that couples systems and leads to inconsistent displays. Instead, have HealthSystem invoke an event with current and max values, and let UI subscribe. Takeaway: centralize health logic, clamp values, and expose change events to decouple UI and gameplay. Ask yourself: if a power-up heals the player, will the health ever exceed its maximum? Use clamping to guarantee it won't.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Health Essentials
Definition

What a HealthSystem contains

  • • maxHealth: a public value set in the editor for tuning difficulty.
  • • currentHealth: an internal value exposed via a read-only property or event.
  • • TakeDamage(amount) and Heal(amount): validated methods that modify health through the setter.
  • • OnHealthChanged events to update UI and other reactions.
Analogy
Think of health as a water tank with a labeled maximum. Damage removes water, healing adds it, but valves keep it between empty and full.
Common mistake
Updating UI from many scripts instead of subscribing to a single health event causes inconsistent displays and harder debugging.
Example
A property setter clamps values and invokes a UnityEvent for UI updates. The code snippet below shows the currentHealth setter used throughout the class.
private int _currentHealth;
public int currentHealth
{
  get { return _currentHealth; }
  private set
  {
    _currentHealth = Mathf.Clamp(value, 0, maxHealth);
    OnHealthChanged?.Invoke(_currentHealth, maxHealth);
    if (_currentHealth <= 0)
    {
      Die();
    }
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Use a clamped setter and events to make health authoritative and observable across systems.

screens.title: TakeDamage and Heal Methods
screens.narratorSegment: TakeDamage and Heal are the public methods players and hazards call to change health. Implement them defensively: immediately return if the incoming amount is negative, because negative damage or negative healing often introduces bugs. Call the clamped currentHealth setter so the single place that enforces limits and triggers events remains authoritative. Add a debug log with the name of the object and resulting health to make early playtests faster to diagnose. For example, when the hazard collides with the player, it should call playerHealth. TakeDamage(damageAmount); the HealthSystem will reduce the private field via the setter, clamp the value, invoke OnHealthChanged, and call Die if needed. For Heal, do the same pattern but increase currentHealth. A common misconception is to perform manual min/max calculations in multiple places. That duplicates logic and risks inconsistencies. Instead, funnel all changes through the property setter. Finally, when testing, trigger damage and healing cases that push values below zero or above max to confirm clamping. Do you have a debug workflow that reveals both the old and new health values when adjusting damage values in play mode?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Damage & Heal
Code Walkthrough

TakeDamage() and Heal()

These methods should guard negative inputs and pass all changes through the clamped setter so behavior remains consistent.

public void TakeDamage(int amount)
{
  if (amount < 0) return; // Prevent healing from negative damage
  currentHealth -= amount;
  Debug.Log(gameObject.name + " took " + amount + " damage. Current health: " + currentHealth);
}

public void Heal(int amount)
{
  if (amount < 0) return; // Prevent damage from negative heal
  currentHealth += amount;
  Debug.Log(gameObject.name + " healed " + amount + " health. Current health: " + currentHealth);
}
Pro-tip
Use descriptive Debug.Log messages that include object names to speed up playtest debugging across multiple enemies.
Watch out
Negative damage or healing that isn't checked can invert behavior unexpectedly and bypass clamping logic.
Example scenario
A SpikeHazard deals 25 damage on collision. The player has 20 current health. TakeDamage reduces health to 0, triggers Die, and the GameManager handles game over. If the player then picks a 50-point health pack, Heal calls the setter and clamps result at maxHealth.
Key Takeaway

Methods validate inputs and rely on a single clamped setter to keep state consistent and observable.

screens.title: Die() and Player Death Handling
screens.narratorSegment: When current health reaches zero the HealthSystem should run Die to centralize death behavior. Die is responsible for invoking OnPlayerDied so other systems can respond, disabling player movement to stop further input, and optionally playing animations or sound. For player-specific behavior, OnPlayerDied is typically observed by the GameManager to switch the global game state to GameOver and pause the game. A common error is placing scene or UI logic inside Die; prefer invoking an event and letting the GameManager or UI system decide whether to display a GameOver panel or restart the level. For example, Die might call GetComponent (). enabled = false and then OnPlayerDied?. Invoke(). The GameManager, which subscribed to that event in Start, receives the callback and executes Time. timeScale = 0f and OnGameOver?. Invoke(), thereby keeping concerns separated. Test this by deliberately dropping the player's health to zero in the editor, watching movement stop, and verifying the GameManager's GameOver flow runs. Think: does Die directly reload the scene, or does it hand responsibility to GameManager? Prefer the latter for single-responsibility. Die() and Player Death Handling means die should stop local behavior and broadcast death; let gamemanager handle global consequences like pausing and restarting.. In practical terms, trigger animations, disable movement, and notify the gamemanager when health hits zero.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Die & Player Death
Definition

Die() responsibilities

  • • Invoke local effects: disable movement, play death animation, stop input.
  • • Emit OnPlayerDied event for global listeners to handle game over.
  • • Avoid global decisions here; delegate UI and scene control to GameManager.
void Die()
{
  Debug.Log(gameObject.name + " has died!");
  OnPlayerDied?.Invoke();
  GetComponent().enabled = false;
  // Play animation or disable renderer here if needed
}
Scenario
Player collides with a SpikeHazard while at low health. Die disables movement and invokes OnPlayerDied. GameManager, which subscribed, pauses the game and triggers GameOver UI. This separation keeps local and global responsibilities clear.
Misconception
Putting scene reloads or UI toggles directly in Die tightly couples the character to global flow and prevents reuse for enemies or NPCs.
Key Takeaway

Let Die stop local behavior and broadcast death; let GameManager decide the global response.

screens.title: UI Integration & Events
screens.narratorSegment: Synchronizing health with UI is best done via events instead of direct calls. Expose a UnityEvent OnHealthChanged that sends current and max health when values update. The UI subscribes to this event and updates a health bar fill amount and text independently. This decoupling makes it safe to change UI layout later without touching HealthSystem logic. For example, your HealthSystem invokes OnHealthChanged(currentHealth, maxHealth) in the setter; a HealthBar script registers a listener and converts the two values into an anchored fill and percentage label. A common mistake is to have multiple scripts try to set the same UI element, which causes race conditions and visual flicker. Another misconception is that events are slower; for typical gameplay they are efficient and dramatically improve code clarity. Test by running the scene, altering health via the console or hazard collisions, and inspecting whether the UI always reflects the clamped values. The final question to consider: if a UI element is missing or unassigned in the Inspector, how will you make the subscription fail gracefully? Use null checks and editor-time warnings. UI Integration & Events means expose health change events; let ui subscribe and render values so systems remain decoupled and easier to maintain.. In practical terms, use unityevents to decouple health logic from ui updates.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › UI & Events
Comparison

Direct calls vs Event-driven

Direct UI calls
Multiple scripts write UI state directly. Tighter coupling and higher chance of inconsistent updates.
Event-driven
HealthSystem emits events and UI subscribes. Clear separation and easier refactoring.
Example
HealthSystem invokes OnHealthChanged(current, max). A HealthBar script listens and sets fill = (float)current / max and updates a percent label. If the HealthBar is missing, use null checks and log a warning to avoid runtime errors.
Pro-tip
Use UnityEvent serialized fields to wire UI in the Inspector so designers can reassign visuals without code changes.
Key Takeaway

Prefer events for UI updates to keep gameplay logic and presentation decoupled and maintainable.

screens.title: Coin & Hazard Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating coins and hazards connects small interactions to global systems. When the player collects a coin, the Coin script should call GameManager. Instance. AddScore(coinValue) then Destroy(gameObject). This keeps scoring centralized. For hazards, the Hazard script should detect collisions, get the player's HealthSystem component, and call TakeDamage(damageAmount) if present. This pattern avoids embedding scoring or health logic inside unrelated scripts. A typical implementation checks tags with CompareTag("Player") to ensure only the player triggers these actions. A common bug is assuming GameManager. Instance always exists; ensure the GameManager is instantiated in Awake before these scripts run. Another issue is calling Destroy on the player or hazard immediately within collision callbacks without considering needed order of operations; prefer disabling the object or queuing destruction if further logic must run. Test by collecting coins and observing log messages and score updates, and by colliding with hazards to see health decrease and death events fire. Always verify that coinValue and damageAmount are positive and that their values are tuned in the Inspector for expected difficulty. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Coins & Hazards
Process

Coin collection and hazard collision

  1. Coin detects player via OnTriggerEnter and CompareTag("Player").
  2. Coin calls GameManager.Instance.AddScore(coinValue) and destroys itself.
  3. Hazard checks collisions, retrieves HealthSystem from the other object, and calls TakeDamage(damageAmount).
  4. HealthSystem processes damage through clamped setter, invokes events, and triggers Die if needed.
Code snippets
// Coin.cs
void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
{
  if (other.CompareTag("Player"))
  {
    GameManager.Instance.AddScore(coinValue);
    Destroy(gameObject);
  }
}

// Hazard.cs
void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
{
  if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Player"))
  {
    HealthSystem playerHealth = collision.gameObject.GetComponent();
    if (playerHealth != null) playerHealth.TakeDamage(damageAmount);
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Thin interaction scripts call centralized systems so behavior stays consistent and easy to tune.

screens.title: Singleton GameManager Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: The Singleton pattern guarantees only one instance of the GameManager exists and provides a global access point. In Unity you implement this in Awake: check if Instance is already set; if so and it's not this, destroy the duplicate. Otherwise assign Instance = this and call DontDestroyOnLoad so the GameManager persists across scenes. Store global data like score and UnityEvents for OnScoreChanged and OnGameOver on the GameManager. Callers then use GameManager. Instance. AddScore(100) without needing references set in the Inspector. Important safety notes: initialize the Instance in Awake rather than Start, because other scripts' Start or Awake may need the Instance during their initialization. Avoid circular dependencies where GameManager calls into scripts that reference GameManager in their Awake; prefer subscribing in Start or using explicit initialization ordering. Test for duplication by creating multiple GameManager prefabs and ensuring only one remains at runtime. If Instance is null when accessed, the usual cause is initialization order mistakes; move setup to Awake to fix this. The architecture keeps global control centralized and simplifies subscribing to game-wide events like OnGameOver. Singleton GameManager Pattern means initialize instance in awake, use dontdestroyonload, and centralize global state to avoid duplication and access errors.. In practical terms, ensure a single persistent manager controls score and global game state.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › GameManager Singleton
Architecture

Singleton responsibilities

  • • Expose public static Instance for global access.
  • • Persist across scenes with DontDestroyOnLoad.
  • • Manage score, game state enums, and global UnityEvents.
public static GameManager Instance { get; private set; }

void Awake()
{
  if (Instance != null && Instance != this) Destroy(gameObject);
  else { Instance = this; DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject); }
}
Example methods
public void AddScore(int amount)
{
  if (amount < 0) return;
  score += amount;
  OnScoreChanged?.Invoke(score);
}

public void HandlePlayerDeath()
{
  Time.timeScale = 0f;
  OnGameOver?.Invoke();
}
Safety note
Avoid accessing GameManager.Instance in other scripts' Awake if the Instance may not exist yet. Initialize critical subscriptions in Start or ensure order explicitly.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Events & Subscriptions
Code Walkthrough

Subscribing in Start

void Start()
{
  GameObject player = GameObject.FindGameObjectWithTag("Player");
  if (player != null)
  {
    HealthSystem playerHealth = player.GetComponent();
    if (playerHealth != null) playerHealth.OnPlayerDied.AddListener(HandlePlayerDeath);
  }
  OnScoreChanged?.Invoke(score);
}
If GameManager persists across scenes, use SceneManager.sceneLoaded to re-wire listeners for new player instances instead of double-subscribing in Start each scene load.
Practical checks
  • • Log subscription events to verify single registration.
  • • Guard against null when finding the player in Start.
  • • Reset or re-wire subscriptions when scenes reload to reference new objects.
Key Takeaway

Manage subscriptions carefully with persistent managers to prevent duplicated handlers and missing references across scenes.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Debugging
screens.narratorSegment: When building health and game state systems, certain mistakes recur. First, initializing Singletons in Start rather than Awake leads to null Instance errors when other scripts access the manager early. Fix this by moving initialization to Awake. Second, allowing negative or out-of-range values in TakeDamage or Heal creates inverted behaviors; prevent this by validating inputs and always using Mathf. Clamp. Third, subscribing multiple times across scene loads causes handlers to run multiple times; track subscriptions or rewire after scene load to avoid duplication. Fourth, tight coupling—updating UI from many places—creates inconsistencies; prefer event-driven UI updates. To debug, use descriptive Debug. Log statements showing object names and resulting values whenever health or score changes. Use breakpoints or temporary test buttons to force damage and healing to exercise edge cases like exactly zero or exactly max. Ask: if the GameManager is persistent, does it re-subscribe on every scene load? If so, where should you move the subscription logic to prevent duplicates? These checks speed debugging and help you ship a stable prototype. screens.title: Restarting Levels and Resetting State
screens.narratorSegment: Restarting a level requires careful resetting of game state and time scale. When the GameManager detects player death, HandlePlayerDeath can set Time. timeScale to zero to pause the simulation and invoke OnGameOver for UI to display. To restart, call RestartLevel which sets Time. timeScale back to one and reloads the active scene. Also reset persistent variables like score so a fresh session begins cleanly. If GameManager persists across loads, ensure it detects scene reloads and re-finds the Player to re-subscribe to events. Avoid destroying the GameManager on reload unless you explicitly want a fresh manager. A common mistake is relying on automatic re-initialization and forgetting to reset score or other global counters, resulting in carry-over between runs. Test restart by triggering death, confirming the game pauses, then invoking RestartLevel and verifying score resets and health initializes to max. Think about UX: often a small delay or a confirmation before restarting improves player experience and avoids abrupt restarts during accidental deaths. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these core ideas in mind as you implement health and global game logic. First, a Health System should centralize current and maximum health, clamp changes, and emit events when values change so UI and other systems can react reliably. Second, game state is a global mode the game occupies—Playing, Paused, GameOver—and transitions should be coordinated centrally. Third, the GameManager should be a Singleton initialized in Awake and persisted with DontDestroyOnLoad so it serves as a single authoritative coordinator for score and state. Each of these concepts reduces bugs and makes the game easier to extend: event-driven health updates decouple UI from gameplay, clamping prevents invalid values, and a persistent manager prevents duplicated logic. As you code, test edge cases: negative inputs, multiple subscriptions, and scene restarts. These checks catch the most frequent errors and lead to a sturdier, more maintainable prototype.

In this lesson you will learn how to give characters a clear life cycle and how to coordinate the whole game's state. We'll define what a health system tracks, how to safely apply damage and healing so values never go out of bounds, and how to surface those changes to UI and gameplay events. Then we'll introduce a single authoritative GameManager using the Singleton pattern to track score, subscribe to player death, and move the game between Playing and GameOver states. This matters because predictable health behavior prevents bugs like negative health or overhealing, while a single GameManager prevents duplicated logic and keeps transitions consistent across scenes. As a concrete example, you'll implement a HealthSystem script that clamps current health between zero and a maximum, fires events on change, and calls Die when health reaches zero. Then you'll create a GameManager that persists across scene loads, exposes AddScore, and pauses the game on player death. Watch for common mistakes: initializing Singletons in the wrong lifecycle method and allowing negative or out-of-range values. By the end, you'll be able to wire coins, hazards, health, and score together in a robust way.

Each objective includes a small, practical skill: writing the TakeDamage and Heal methods so health never leaves the 0-to-max range; using events to update health bars; and coding Awake to establish a Singleton that persists across scenes. Clamp to prevent overheal or negative life. Keep these core ideas in mind as you implement health and global game logic. First, a Health System should centralize current and maximum health, clamp changes, and emit events when values change so UI and other systems can react reliably. Second, game state is a global mode the game occupies—Playing, Paused, GameOver—and transitions should be coordinated centrally. Third, the GameManager should be a Singleton initialized in Awake and persisted with DontDestroyOnLoad so it serves as a single authoritative coordinator for score and state. Each of these concepts reduces bugs and makes the game easier to extend: event-driven health updates decouple UI from gameplay, clamping prevents invalid values, and a persistent manager prevents duplicated logic. As you code, test edge cases: negative inputs, multiple subscriptions, and scene restarts. These checks catch the most frequent errors and lead to a sturdier, more maintainable prototype.

Remember these three succinct rules as you build and iterate. First, clamp health with Mathf. Clamp and funnel changes through one setter so death and UI notifications are consistent. Second, use UnityEvents to decouple presentation from logic: health and score systems should broadcast changes and let UI respond. Third, implement the GameManager as a Singleton initialized in Awake and persisted with DontDestroyOnLoad so scene transitions and global events behave predictably. These practices reduce bugs, simplify tuning, and make it faster to add features like lives, power-ups, or level meta. Before finishing, run tests that push health below zero and above max, cause the GameManager to restart the scene, and verify that score resets. Keeping these checks in your standard playtest routine will let your prototype scale without hidden, persistent state issues.
